p1.title: Passage 1
paras: We usually think of reading as a journey with a destination: we begin a book in order to finish it, and once the last page is turned, the book is done with. Rereading upsets this idea. A novel read at eighteen and again at forty is, in an important sense, two different books, because the reader who returns to it has changed. Passages once skimmed as dull may now seem the heart of the story; a character once admired may now appear foolish or cruel. The words on the page have not altered, but the experience that the reader brings to them has.

For this reason, rereading is not the idle habit of those who have run out of new books. It is one of the few ways in which we can measure our own growth, for the familiar text becomes a fixed point against which our shifting judgements are revealed. It also rewards attention in a way that a first reading rarely can. Freed from the anxiety of discovering what happens next, the rereader notices how the effect was achieved: the hint planted early, the sentence that does more work than it seemed to. In an age that measures reading by the number of titles completed, the quiet return to an old book may be the more demanding and the more rewarding discipline.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Financial behavior among youngsters has undergone considerable transformation in the digital era. Easy access to online banking, digital wallets, instant credit systems, and e-commerce platforms has made financial transactions more convenient than ever before. However, financial experts argue that such convenience has also encouraged impulsive spending and weakened the traditional culture of savings among young people. Many adolescents and young professionals increasingly associate financial success with visible consumption rather than disciplined wealth management. Social media platforms further intensify this trend by promoting luxury lifestyles and instant gratification. Economists warn that inadequate financial literacy at an early age can lead to long-term debt dependency and poor investment decisions. Consequently, educational institutions and financial organizations have begun introducing programs on budgeting, saving, taxation, and responsible borrowing. Advocates of financial education believe that cultivating saving habits during youth not only improves individual economic security but also contributes to broader economic stability within society.

questions.q: The central claim of the passage is that:
opts: Young readers usually misunderstand the novels they read.
Rereading is valuable because it reveals both the craft of a book and the growth of its reader.
A first reading of a book is of little worth.
People should stop reading new books altogether.
questions.why: Main idea: rereading lets us 'measure our own growth' and notice 'how the effect was achieved'.

questions.q: According to the passage, the rereader notices how effects were achieved because he or she is:
opts: Freed from the anxiety of discovering what happens next.
Guided by the comments of literary critics.
Reading a revised edition of the text.
Reading more slowly with advancing age.
questions.why: Detail: 'Freed from the anxiety of discovering what happens next, the rereader notices how the effect was achieved'.

questions.q: The author would most likely disagree with which statement?
opts: The best measure of a reader is the number of books he or she has completed.
Rereading can reveal changes in one's own judgement.
A familiar text can serve as a fixed point of comparison.
A first reading is often driven by curiosity about the plot.
questions.why: Inference: the author contrasts 'an age that measures reading by the number of titles completed' with the 'more rewarding discipline' of rereading.

questions.q: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to:
opts: Contrast a quantity-based view of reading with the value of returning to old books.
Criticise the authors of old books.
Urge readers to complete more titles each year.
Announce that reading is in decline.
questions.why: Purpose: it sets 'the number of titles completed' against 'the quiet return to an old book'.

questions.q: The word "idle" in "the idle habit" most nearly means:
opts: Broken
Purposeless
Unemployed
Silent
questions.why: Vocabulary: the author denies that rereading is a pointless pastime of those with nothing better to read; 'unemployed' is a different sense of idle.

questions.q: What is the primary concern expressed in the passage?
opts: Decline in online banking systems
Increasing influence of technology on agriculture
Weakening savings habits among youngsters
Excessive government regulation of financial institutions
questions.why: Third sentence sets the concern. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Professor, Livestock Production and Management), May 2026.

questions.q: According to the passage, social media contributes to
opts: responsible financial planning
promotion of consumption-oriented lifestyles
decline in digital transactions
reduction of financial inequality

questions.q: Which assumption is most strongly implied in the passage?
opts: Financial literacy can positively influence long-term economic behaviour
Youngsters should avoid digital payments completely
Traditional banking is superior to modern systems
Economic growth depends entirely on government
questions.why: Programmes on budgeting and saving are offered because literacy changes behaviour. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Professor, Livestock Production and Management), May 2026.

questions.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
opts: Technology alone causes youth unemployment
Financial education has become increasingly important in modern society
Savings habits are irrelevant in digital economies
Social media should be legally banned

questions.q: The phrase “instant gratification” most nearly refers to
opts: delayed financial rewards
immediate satisfaction of desires
government financial assistance
long-term investment planning
questions.why: Gratification = satisfaction; instant = immediate. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Professor, Livestock Production and Management), May 2026.
